title: New Orleans dance halls and the killing of Billy Phillips
summary: Carew recalls looking into rough dance halls and the murder of Billy Phillips, who ran the 101 Ranch.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Did you get in, when you were in New Orleans, did you get into any of those dance halls down there? Well, I used to look in on them.

I never, I kind of went out to be strolling around, of course they were playing good jazz there in those places. They were pretty rough places, weren't they? Well, they were, they were, well, there was a pretty heavy crowd, you may say, the roughnecks that did that. But I don't recall any disturbance except when they killed Billy Phillips. And that was rough that night. That's Billy Phillips. Yeah, he ran the 101 Ranch. The competition was right across the street at the tuxedo competition. And the story was then, as they tried to develop it, that somebody had hired Chip the Blood and Lefty Louie to come down from New Orleans and bump Billy Phillips off, which he did. And they, but they never caught him and they never hung in on him. It wasn't a few days that both dance halls were still going, were going again. The, the state or the areas that Billy Phillips kept on having the dance hall running. Well, I used to pass by and I'd take a look in there and see what was going on. They, they were, as I say, there was never any rough stuff. There was a very heavy, rough crowd all right, rough necks. And I don't know that they ever had any other activities there. The girls there to dance with the fellas. They danced and they, they got into buying drinks, which is no, a gang of course. But I don't think they had any other activities at that time. They stayed strictly in the dance hall. There's nothing, no connection with any other place that I knew of. And, as I say, there was, I don't recall any other writhing or rough stuff of that time, except when they killed Billy Phillips. But there were three of them that played regularly. And that, that was the only, there was the two, the Tuxedo and the 101 Ranch, and then a place on the next corner back, because as near as I can figure, was Eddie Grosselles. Eddie Grosselles. And that was, that was built for, for that purpose. It was built in the dance hall, and I think King Oliver played in there. I'm very sure he did, because it was the only one. And I was passing by there one night, and there was, the band was playing a very hot piece. And they were just finishing up. And I, I said, well, I want to know what that is. And they were just finishing dancing. And I walked in, I walked the full length of the dance hall, and went my way through the dance, and right back to the player's platform. And King Oliver, I'm sure, was standing up in front there. He just got tootin' tootin' his trumpet. And I said, what's the name of that tune you just played? And he said, that's Chicken Reel. It's a stop-time piece too, you know. They blast out on that . Whatever. It goes on and strong there, Chicken Reel. It was taken from an old folk song. The verse . Well, you know, Doc Sushan said that King Oliver didn't want anybody to know what he was playing. he was playing and when he was a kid, he was a kid with these other boys, he would ask Joe what he was playing and he would always answer the name of the tune, who shot John? Same tune. I guess the present day writers of jazz information and so forth, I think it's funny that I didn't go up and ask who was playing, but I never did. I said, what is that? Tony Jackson was the only one that I made an effort to find out who he was and who in the world was that? I told Hulseiser, I think it was, Hulseiser wrote me and said, do you think that so and so played so and so and so? I wrote him and I said, I never concerned myself as who was playing. For instance, I'd be on the street and alone come a pretty nice... ...curt to me to run out there and ask the bass drummer what his name was. You mean marching band? Yeah, marching band. I said I was enjoying music as far as chasing him up to find out who was playing the bass drum or anything else. Were these usually parades or... No, it could be anything. It's remarkable now. I know before 1910, before 1909, I knew that the music was somehow different. I remember standing on Canal Street one night near Royal. Royal Street was the street where General said that the bar rooms opened up and threw away the keys. They kept going right through it. There was always life down Royal Street. Purely in the bar room sense, you know. Billiard Hall, too, and something like that. But anyhow, I was standing on Canal Street right close to Royal. I couldn't look down. I was close enough so that I could hear it all of a sudden. A nice, pretty, pretty raucous and good, in that sense. Good jazz group coming up there. I thought, boy, this is pretty good. I see what this is. So I stood there waiting for them to come out of Royal Street. And here came about four guys. Yeah. One with a tuba, one with a trumpet. Another with something else. And they were making all kinds of music, you know. Jim and the Prince was it. And it was surprising me. I had a laugh. But it was good. Did you see any ride on the wagon? Huh? Did you see any band ride on the wagon? Well, they used to do that more on the Mardi Gras time or something like that. You know, they'd get out and drag them around town because they'd kill themselves trying to walk all day. They would get in wagons then. And to be around town, of course, now on picnics, they would take the band out and they'd be in the wagon while they were on a picnic. And in 1910, we had a salesman at the Remington Company by the name of Carroll. He was so good that the company promoted him to be manager in Cincinnati. So he went up there for a couple of years, but he didn't like Cincinnati after New Orleans. He'd rather be back in New Orleans. I think he was a native New Orleans man. So by 1911 sometime, he was back in New Orleans. And he brought back a friend from Cincinnati down in New Orleans. And they were working with the Remington Company. And we were on Gravier Street right then, just off of Barone. And one Saturday afternoon, I was working on the books. And up Barone Street comes a good-sized, real legitimate band. Oh, they've been playing hot stuff, you know, coming up. And Carroll stood up immediately. He walked to that front door and stepped out on the walk and watched them go by. And he stepped back in and he said to his friend from Cincinnati, he says, that's music you won't hear anywhere else in the United States. That was no later than 1912, very late, because after that I wasn't a bookkeeper. I went on the road myself then. But he was wise to that. He hadn't heard any of that in Cincinnati. And I know in 1909, which was probably the year I stopped off in Chicago, and I was on the way to visit relatives in Michigan, Grand Rapids. And in Grand Rapids while I was there, the Scotty Band, which was a famous band, I guess they were from Scotland, they'd been playing in Canada and they came through Grand Rapids and they gave a little parade one day and stopped in Campaw Square in the center of the town and played. I happened to be downtown at the time with my niece. We stood there and watched and listened to them playing two or three numbers. I said, well, it's his. Their outfits in New Orleans have got six or eight pieces, can make more of a show than they can. So, people took it for granted, you know. They weren't worrying about, of course, if they had friends playing, whether they got to, you know, the way they got acquainted with the people that played, they'd say, well, five players, and so on.
Plus the musicians all remember who played, but nobody else does down there from that period, I guess.
Well, the friends of the players knew, even the players themselves, they played with these people and all that.
